result.cardAnatomy: Portrait 2:3 cover, full-bleed with rounded corners, high-gloss anime key art (usually 1-2 characters). The title is painted into the art as a logo, webtoon or light-novel style, on creator titles as well as Originals. Overlays: a rank number in a dark square at top-left on ranked rows; a lime '*ORIGINAL' pill at top-right on official titles; a small round gallery icon when the title has scene images (Hero Academy Apex, 0 images, has none). Under the cover: the title in plain text (up to 2 lines), then a single meta line such as '48.5M · OOC', which is the lifetime message count plus the creator name. Cards show no likes, comments, tags or genre. The data behind each card includes w200/w600 webp covers plus gif/gif600/mp4 animated versions: 67 of the 109 home carousel cards have an animated asset. The web build is in experiment 'ooc_video_thumbnail' group A and showed static covers. One-liners often advertise how much content a title has, e.g. '[images 600+ / female 14 / male 7]' or '+300 imgs / 21 characters'. The story page adds a creator chip; chips for image count ('150 Images'), prompt type ('Creator Custom Prompt'), target and genre; a one-liner; hashtags; counters (48.5M messages, 130K likes, 169.7K comments) and a 'New Play' button. Below that: an Avatar (persona) picker, a Starting Scenarios dropdown (Lumencia has Character Preview / Enrollment / Free Mode, 50 images each), a prologue preview, and a long markdown description with image galleries, cast lists, BGM notes and slash-command cheat sheets (/event, /anti-impersonation). Comments come last, sorted by likes.

mechanics: Credits economy. New accounts get 500 credits, and a 'Sign up and get 500 credits!' tooltip sits on every page. Packs: 2,000 for $2.29 web / $2.89 app; 10,300 for $11.49 / $14.49 (marked recommended); 21,000 for $22.49 / $28.49; 53,500 for $56.49 / $71; 110,000 for $113.99 / $142.99. Web is about 20% cheaper (Stripe checkout). The premium 'Apex' mode costs 90 credits a message (78 during its launch sale), about $0.10. A 'Max' mode also exists.
Daily check-in in a 'Claim Free Credits' tab: 300 credits a day, doubled to 600 for Halloween (Oct 25-31).

Free Messages event (Nov 10-30): 7 free messages on every OOC Original the player hasn't played, including Originals released during the event and for players who join mid-event. It ran before from Oct 29 to Nov 8.

Welcome Mission onboarding checklist (a banner on Home for signed-in users): browse the ranking, visit personalization, complete a chat, do the daily check-in. Each step triggers a 'Welcome Mission N Success!' toast. There are also tutorial and onboarding status checks.

Referral codes (since Oct 14): the new player gets 500 credits, and the referrer earns 5% of that player's credit purchases in their first 30 days, paid in credits. An optional setting adds the code to every story link a player shares.
Gacha-style limited bundles. The Halloween Candy Pack was 70,000 credits plus a random bonus: +7,777 (55%), +10,000 (40%), +50,000, up to +1,000,000.

Creator economy. Since June, Official Creators earn a share of the credits their stories bring in. The OOC Originals program (open to Certified Creators 18+ since Nov 18) buys a title outright for $200 ($500 in the Halloween round) plus 5% of paid credits, paid monthly and capped at $1M. Selected titles get a home-screen row, a notification to the creator's followers and a release on the Korean and Japanese sister apps; the announcement says a sister-app top earner makes over $45k a month. Fan fiction, Utility and NSFW titles are not eligible.

Social features: follow creators (profiles show follower counts; OOC has 127.6k); a profile Feed for posts with likes and comment threads (since Sep 21); Series, which group sequels and can be subscribed to (Nov 18); notifications; 'has-new' badges.

Comments on every story, sorted by likes, with replies and pinned comments. The top comments on #1 Lumencia are 'Please like my comment for credits' (3,281 likes), 'Follow for follow' (1,879) and 'F4F, lets help each other get credits'. Players treat likes and follows as a route to credits or creator status, which inflates the public engagement numbers. I couldn't see the exact rule logged out.

Collection loops: collectible endings and ending cards (Psychic Academy NOVA has 30), shareable epilogues, and a scene-image gallery per starting scenario with 'has-new' flags. Since Nov 11 a starting scenario can hold up to 1,600 scene images, laid out as a character-by-emotion table.

Play tools: several starting scenarios per story, a persona picker, session branching (Sep 17), writing style, regeneration instructions and thinking depth (Nov 5), slash commands inside stories (/event, /anti-impersonation), suggested replies, and an AIRPG game mode ('Dice of Fate').
Leaderboards everywhere: Top 100 Rankings and New Ranking (Daily/Weekly/Monthly x All/Female/Male), numbered Top Ranked and Trending Now rows, and a Popular Searches top 10.
Personalization: every page request carries a target audience (male/female), rankings filter by Female- or Male-oriented, and visiting personalization is a Welcome Mission step.

Seasonal live ops: a Halloween reskin of tabs, app icon and launch screen; a home section fed automatically by #Halloween titles; double check-in; themed credit packs. An announcement lands about every 4 days.

Sign-in is only required to act. Browsing, story pages, rankings, search and comments are public; Credits and My Titles redirect to Google or Apple sign-in. The sign-in screen's tagline is literally 'THE PLAYABLE ANIME', the same positioning as Plotbreak.
whyItFeelsLively: Sheer density. The Main tab stacks 6 hero slides, 16 genre chips, 6 card rows (109 cards, 87 unique) and an 11-tag row before an endless 6-column grid. Every genre tab has its own hero and grid, and the two ranking tabs each hold 6 filterable Top 100s. A user never reaches the end.

Most rows are numbered or tied to a time window. Top Ranked and Trending Now show rank numbers, and the rankings run daily, weekly and monthly, so the page reads like a live chart that changes every day.

A steady supply of official titles. OOC has released 539 Originals in 7 months, in drops of 9-25 (five drops between Nov 2 and Nov 17). Each drop fills the hero, the New OOC Originals row and Trending Now, and 7 free messages per unplayed Original pull players into it. Today all 10 Trending Now titles are Originals 4-9 days old.

Plenty of user-made titles underneath: about 450-650 new public stories a day from about 400 creators. Two creator rows are random samples that reshuffle on every load, so a refresh visibly changes the page.

Big public numbers. Every card shows a lifetime message count (48.5M, 21.6M, 20.7M) and every story page shows likes and comments (130K / 169.7K). Players trade likes and follows for credits ('like my comment for credits', F4F), which pushes those counters higher still.

Covers look like a webtoon storefront: the title is painted into glossy anime key art on almost every card, creator titles included. 67 of the 109 home cards also have animated cover versions being tested.

Each title looks like a lot of content. One-liners advertise image and cast counts ('600+ images / 14 F / 7 M'), endings and background music, and official titles carry 50-1,600 scene images and versioned updates (Lumencia is on v20).
Something is always new or time-limited: 20 announcements in 11 weeks (events, features, sales), seasonal reskins, and hashtag-fed seasonal sections.

Tight genre focus with two audiences. The catalog leans on proven tropes (academy, isekai, harem, hero vs villain, revenge and cheating), and a separate female-oriented track (romance fantasy, BL/HL routes, reverse harem) shows up through the gender filter. Fan fiction is kept off Home, so the storefront looks like an original, ownable catalog.
blockers: The Credits and My Titles pages redirect to sign-in, and I did not sign in. Check-in amounts, Welcome Mission rewards, the rule behind 'like my comment for credits', and per-message prices for the default models therefore come from public announcements and the site's JavaScript, not from using the features. The Apex price (90 credits, 78 on sale) is from the Oct 23 announcement, and the chat-model price endpoint returned 404.

read_network_requests only captured image requests. The data came from the page's own query cache and read-only GET requests to api.ooc.ai made from inside the page (pages, stories, rankings, search, announcements, keyword ranking, credit products). Nothing was written, liked, posted or purchased.

There is no total-count endpoint, so the 50-65k story figure is an extrapolation from search counts. I couldn't estimate the character count reliably because character search also matches descriptions.

The web always queries safe-only content and defaults the audience to male, so NSFW titles and app-only features are not covered: Series and Originals submission need iOS app v0.1.30+, video thumbnails only show in the app or a test group, and the iOS app has hidden NSFW since Nov 12.

verification.overall: The first pass's headline numbers hold up within about half a point when recomputed from different sources. Those sources were DB auth.users (the anonymous sessions created on a fresh install), the turns table instead of the wallet ledger, and PostHog keyed by person instead of install id. About 30 installs a day is right (30.5 to 30.7, and 35 to 44 a day over the last two weeks), but only about 25 sign in and about 12.5 ever play. D1 is about 5% for accounts, 7.6% for players and 11% for any open. D7 is about 1% for accounts and players and 3.6% for any open. Two findings need correcting. First, the credits conclusion is wrong. The new-user grant is exactly 10 turns, and day-0 play piles up at exactly 10 and 15 turns in both the DB and PostHog. 'Turn 10' in the funnel is therefore the credit wall, not an engagement milestone. Players who end day 0 out of credits come back to play about a quarter as often as equally deep players who still have credits (small n, observational). Replace 'no visible harm' with 'likely harm, A/B the grant'. Second, 'every retention measure slipped' is overstated. D1 and the 7-day return are flat from P1 to P2, and only exact-day-7 is down, at borderline significance. The onboarding-to-first-run leak (about 38%, roughly 9 to 10 people a day) is confirmed. It splits into 136 people who never open a story page and 161 who open one and back out, and each half is about the size of the later drops. Calendar-day D1 also reads about 1.6x higher than a strict 24 to 48 hour window (5.2% vs 3.3%). Everything was read-only: SELECT queries, HogQL, and reading code and docs. No files were created. playCost.basis:
Data: 561 turn.generated log lines pulled read-only from Railway (plotbreak-api, 4 deployments, 2026-11-18 to 2026-11-22). Each line carries inputTokens, cachedTokens and outputTokens; I priced them at today's OpenAI list rates.

Session model: turn n input I_n = P + (n−1)Δ.
- P = 9,300: median input of the first logged turn when cold, n=101 sessions.
- Δ = 450: median input growth between consecutive turns, n=456.
For 20 turns: ΣI = 20×9,300 + 450×190 = 271,500. Cached = 253,650 (the previous request each turn). Uncached = 17,850, billed at the 1.25× write rate.
VIVID: 17,850 × $2.50 + 253,650 × $0.20 + 12,120 × $12, per M = $0.0446 + $0.0507 + $0.1454 = $0.241.
Output is 60% of the bill, so the beat length matters more than the context.

Caching notes:
- The append-only shape (narrator.ts:915-927) keeps the prefix byte-identical. 82.9% of live VIVID input tokens were cache hits.
- GPT-5.6 bills cache writes at 1.25× and reads at 0.1×.
- Production sends prompt_cache_retention '24h' (turn-service.ts:320 → openai.ts:266). OpenAI's docs say GPT-5.6 replaced that parameter with prompt_cache_options.ttl (30m default, 12h at a 2.5× write), so the 24h setting is probably ignored (UNVERIFIED). Consistent with that, 25 of 460 non-first turns (5.4%) came back fully uncached.
- Moving to a 12h TTL would add ≈$0.045 per 20-turn session in writes to avoid ~1 miss worth $0.03, so it is roughly break-even.
- Arcs keep context under 260K, below the 272K long-context step where terra input costs $4/M (docs/arcs.md).

risks: Copyright and trademark. 3 of the 27 official stories are fan IP: Itachi (Naruto), Ace (One Piece), Light (Death Note). In the last 30 days they took 10.6% of turns (606) and 121 of 901 sessions. Many trending ooc premises are fan fiction too. The bot must take only the trope and fantasy and replace names, designs, costumes, power systems, places and plot specifics. A close paraphrase is still derivative. Apple App Review 5.2.1 bars third-party IP without permission, and store pages and ads raise trademark risk. ooc's own user-written blurbs are other creators' copyrighted text, and scraping them may break ooc's terms. Feed the bot abstract signals only (tags, tropes, counts), never their prose.

Engagement says quality matters more than volume. Last 30 days: official original stories held 7.6 turns per session, user-made Create stories 4.3, fan-IP stories 5.0. These are correlations confounded by shelf placement, but they suggest a compile-grade bot story may underperform. That argues for official-grade text and/or tier (c) review.

There is no automated quality gate at publish time today. checkStoryClarity (narrative-clarity.ts:346) is never called outside specs. Both publish paths hardcode clarity_passed=true (repo/postgres.ts:1971, infra/scripts/migrate.ts:158). checkNarrativeClarity runs only in smoke.ts:165/349 and checks premise and opening clarity, not fun. The bar in authoring-principles.md and BUILD_STATUS.md (about 20 fields per major character, 3+ distinct voice samples, the 'strip the speaker names' test) is human judgement; an LLM judge only approximates it.

Content filters. Image moderation refused Ace's cover twice until minors were described by costume rather than age (generate-art.ts:11-25; RECIPE.md minors rule). Seedream blocks Naruto and One Piece costume sets (MEMORY.md). On text, about 9 of 22 churned day-one runs ended right after the storyteller refused or lectured (story-test.ts:4-10). Trending ooc content skews romantic, and a bot-made story never gets the ALL_IN_ROMANCE paragraph unless a human adds it to the allowlist (story-test.ts).

Dare cannot run unattended. It is reached through an 'Unofficial MCP' tied to a user login, and that session was already expired during this run. Use direct APIs instead: OpenAI gpt-image-2.5/2.6, already wired into create-art.ts, or Seedream via BytePlus and Nano Banana Pro via Gemini at ~$0.09–0.134 per image (UNVERIFIED third-party prices).

Production cost numbers are wrong. costOf (gateway/openai.ts:691-695) bills every input token at the full rate and uses stale prices (openai.ts:52-56 has terra at $1.25/$10, while the list price is $2/$12). luna and sol have no entry at all, so they report $0. In PostHog turn_completed.providerCostUsd, VIVID shows ≈$0.043 per turn against a true $0.022–0.025 (1.7–1.9× over), and QUICK/APEX show $0. docs/analytics.md:86 calls the figure exact. Image telemetry uses $40/M (media/gateway.ts:75) where the list price is $30/M, and leaves out input tokens. Do not budget the bot from these numbers.

Shared OpenAI account. Running out of OpenAI credit has already stopped every production turn once (docs/blocked-on-credits.md). Give the bot its own project, key and hard budget so it cannot starve player turns. gpt-image-2.5-flare is also limited to 20 images per minute on the Build tier.

Shipping path. Official stories are TypeScript fixtures that go through code review, npm run migrate and a deploy. 1–10 stories a day cannot ride that path, so bot output should publish through the Create/DB path (story_versions rows) under an official account.

Unpublished image prices. OpenAI lists no per-image price for gpt-image-2.5/2.6, and 'auto' quality varies: portraits ranged from 158 to 1,372 output tokens in the manifest. At high quality, a cover may cost up to ~$0.165 (GPT-Image-2's published 1024x1536 figure).

verification.overall:
The tier arithmetic is right: every per-story and monthly figure reproduces to within $0.1, and most of the code and price claims hold. Code checks confirmed the model roles, calls per step, batch sizes, retries and the hardcoded clarity_passed flags. OpenAI, Anthropic and Dare list prices match the official pages, and the 30-day database figures match exactly.

Six things change the numbers or the advice:

1. **The repair pass won't get a cache hit.** Opus 5.5's 5-minute cache expires during a ~45K-token generation. The repair costs about $0.53 instead of $0.31, so official-grade costs $2.17 at (a) and $2.68 at (b), not $1.95 and $2.46. Monthly at (b)/(c): $80, $241 and $803 at 1, 3 and 10 stories a day.

2. **Covers aren't only made on Dare.** The newest official world and the v5 covers used OpenAI. The manifest says Dare for every cover because the install script hardcodes it. The v5 script also draws two candidates per story by default. Since Dare can't run unattended, pricing covers through the OpenAI path gives about $0.21 and $1.99 at (a), and $0.47 and $2.35 at (b).

3. **On serving, the "upper bound" is the real price.** The repo's own experiments show 97–99% of uncached GPT-5.6 input is billed at the cache-write rate, so VIVID costs about $0.025 a turn.
   - On live traffic, output is 29% of VIVID spend, not 60%.
   - Cache misses after gaps of more than 30 minutes add about 19% to the VIVID per-turn cost. This also strongly suggests the 24h retention setting is being ignored.
   - A 12h cache would raise spend about 32%, not break even.
   - Monthly serving is about $102–114, best estimate $114, not $108–120.

4. **The smoke test is 16 probes, not 15:** $0.016 per world.

5. **The credit outage doc covers playtests, not production.**

OOC: The Playable Anime is Wrtn Technologies' English edition of Crack (Korea, standalone launch April 2025) and Kyarapu (Japan). Wrtn is based in Seoul, was founded in 2021, and is run by CEO Seyoung Lee. The App Store seller is New AI Entertainment Inc., and press goes to "Wrtn Technologies Inc. (OOC)". OOC launched in North America on 2026-04-15 on iOS, Android and web (Business Wire release, Yahoo mirror: https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/wrtn-technologies-unveils-ai-interactive-210000072.html).

TEAM: about 170-179 employees across all of Wrtn (TheVC / national pension data, Jul-Aug 2026: 107 hires and 50 departures in 12 months). No headcount for OOC alone is public.

FUNDING: about $166M of primary equity (Sacra), including a Series B of about $100M in March 2025 led by Goodwater and a Series C closed 2026-08-26. Reported Series C figures conflict: $72-100M at a valuation of about $722-870M.

FINANCIALS: Wrtn's 2025 revenue was KRW 47.1B (about $33-36M, roughly 15x YoY) on an operating loss of about KRW 58.9B. The 2026 target is about $145M. In April 2026, Crack plus Kyarapu made more than $8M a month on fewer than 500K MAU, about $16-17 per MAU (https://sacra.com/c/wrtn/). Crack users average about 2 h/day, and paying-user retention is above 70% (https://www.woshipm.com/?p=6441577).

OOC REVENUE AND DOWNLOADS (all estimates):
- Sacra says OOC reached $7.2M/month in August 2026, the month overseas revenue first passed domestic. That figure may include Japan.

- iOS rating 4.6 from 14-15.7K ratings, ranked #29-38 in US Entertainment. Google Play 4.2 from 10K+ reviews.

CATALOG: OOC's own figures (Oct 2026) are 52,630 stories, 58,848 characters and 409 first-party Originals.

HOME FEED (ooc.ai, observed 2026-11-21):

ECONOMY:

CREATORS: Certified Creators get 2% of credits spent on their titles for one year. The Originals program buys picked stories for $500 each (October 2026) plus a revenue share, and since 2026-11-18 that covers sequels too.

tactics.tactic: 1. Make the first session a story, not a menu: get a new user into a top story within about 60 seconds, on the best model, with no credit wall or ads before the first cliffhanger
tactics.whatTheyDo: OOC sign-up takes 10 seconds through Google or Apple and gives 500 credits. Character mode is unlimited and free on the Basic model, and Originals hand out free messages during events. After ending open chat for under-18s, Character.AI built its fallback product, Stories: pick 2-3 characters and a genre, the premise is generated, and the player makes frequent choices. Bside found its story ('adventure') sessions retain better than its chat. Chai and Crack treat the model behind those first turns as a retention lever and cut friction for new users (Chai halved ad load).
tactics.evidence: Bside (Kotoko AI, internal, July 2026): on 7-day return, adventure days beat chat days by 5.4 percentage points in all 24 daily cohorts, and about 30% of players active on adventure days come back at D7. Overall D1 is about 60% and D7 about 25%, and 41% of MAU never opened chat. Crack: one model-routing change raised session time by 15% and first-month retention by 10%. Chai: reward-model reranking raised mean conversation length by up to 70%, which gave more than 30% better retention (A/B test, 10K new users a day). Halving ads for new users (from 1 in 8 messages to 1 in 16; more than 20K users, Jan 2025) raised D30 by 18.5% relative, to 19.8%. a16z: generous free tiers produce converted users with higher M3 retention. Chai's 2026 message-limit pop-ups drew reports of users deleting the app.
tactics.effort: Low to Medium (days). Give a new user's first 10-15 turns the top quality tier at no charge. Open every new user on the 2-3 stories with the best D1 in your own data. Move any credit wall, paywall or survey to after the first in-story cliffhanger.
tactics.impact: Highest. Most churn is decided in session one, so this moves D1 most directly, and D7 follows. It is ranked first because Plotbreak is already story-first: the lever is quality and friction in the first 10 minutes, not a new feature.

tactics.tactic: 2. End every session on an open hook, and deliver it as a notification in the character's voice
tactics.whatTheyDo: Character.AI has an 'Away messages' setting that lets bots you've chatted with message you first. Meta tests proactive bot follow-ups with guardrails: only within 14 days of a chat, only after 5 or more user messages, and they stop if the first follow-up goes unanswered. Bside posts the character's activity to a feed while the player is away, which it calls its cheapest AI surface. Webtoon asks readers to subscribe after they finish 3 episodes. It then sends a push and shows an 'UP' badge in four places when a new episode drops. Crack's stories never end: each reply leaves a new conflict or goal.
tactics.evidence: Airship (63M new users, 2017): users who got any push retained nearly 3x (190%) better at 90 days than users who got none or opted out. More than a quarter of 47M opted-in users got no push in their first 90 days, and they retained worse than opt-outs. Media apps showed no significant gain until they sent at least daily. These are correlational vendor figures. Crack users average about 2 h/day on these open loops.
tactics.effort: Low. Plotbreak already schedules a once-a-day local 'story waiting' reminder (/Users/omarlahmimi/Documents/Plotbreak/apps/ios/Plotbreak/Notifications/Reminders.swift), but the body is the same generic line every day: 'Waiting for you to find out what happens next.' Have the production writer (runTurnPure, the streaming path) return a one-line in-character hook with each beat, use the latest one as the notification text, and stop after it is ignored once or twice (Meta's rule). Asking for permission right after the first cliffhanger is a suggestion here, not something a source tested.
tactics.impact: High for D1 to D7. It reuses the user's own unfinished thread, so it works even with a 15-20 story catalog, and it needs no new content.

tactics.tactic: 3. Ship on a fixed weekly schedule: one new story or sequel every week on the same day, with a 'New'/'UP' badge and a push to people who played the prior part
tactics.whatTheyDo: Chapters' listing promises 'new stories and chapters every week', and Episode's promises 'more new stories EVERY WEEK' (150,000+ stories). Webtoon publishes by weekday, sorts each day by views, and spreads popular titles in a genre across the week so a genre's readers come back several times. OOC runs a New Originals row of about 20 recent first-party titles and pushes its newest Originals into Trending. On 2026-11-18 it added Series collections, which group stories into one collection, and began paying creators for sequels.
tactics.evidence: OOC has 409 first-party Originals in about 7 months, alongside 52,630 stories. Its new Originals sit at 18K-131K plays within weeks, and all of Trending Now #1-10 were new Originals on 2026-11-21. Episode: 2.5M storyteller sign-ups and 17K published stories by 2016, about 7M MAU at the time. Kakao and Webtoon built their businesses on weekly serialization (see the benchmarks).
tactics.effort: Medium, and ongoing content work. One release a week. The trend bot or an AI-assisted pipeline can draft it for a human to polish. Plotbreak stories are versioned, and a fixture change needs a new session, so ship next parts as new titles grouped into a Series (OOC's model) rather than editing a live story.
tactics.impact: High for D7 and D30. It fixes the stated root cause, a feed that never changes. It gives every lapsed user a dated reason to return and gives the pushes in tactic 2 something new to announce.

tactics.tactic: 4. A per-story 'wait or pay' timer on top of the daily check-in: the next chapter or free turns unlock on a visible clock, with a reminder when it is ready
tactics.whatTheyDo: Kakao Page's 'Wait-Or-Pay' (2014) gives one free episode, then the next free one after a wait, or you buy to skip. Episode refills 2-4 free passes every 4 hours. Chapters sells 5 tickets for $1.99 and a $0.99 DayPass. OOC gives a 300-credit daily check-in, doubled to 600 during events. Its free credits expire after 30 days, and it shows a first-purchase discount countdown. Chai meters free messages and sells unlimited plans.
tactics.evidence: Kakao says purchase conversion rose to 25% from 3-4% when it switched from selling per episode to Wait-Or-Pay, and Podotree had its first monthly operating profit in four years a month later. An analyst quoted by Asia Business Daily says DAU went from 200K to 900K within a month. Episode App Store reviews complain about waiting about 3 hours for passes, which shows the pull of the timer. OOC's top complaint is the credit wall: a gate needs a free path, or it creates churn instead of returns.
tactics.effort: Low to Medium. Plotbreak already grants 300 free daily credits (the same as OOC) and sends a local reminder for them. What's missing is a per-story clock on the story card and the credit wall ('next chapter free in 4h, or continue now'), plus a reminder when it unlocks.
tactics.impact: High for return frequency (D7 and D30) and the strongest documented paid-conversion lever. Ranked below tactics 1-3 only because the daily check-in, the core of it, already exists.

tactics.tactic: 5. Let new users sample many stories for free, breadth before depth
tactics.whatTheyDo: OOC ran 'Free Messages' twice in a month: 2026-10-29 to 11-08, then 11-10 to 11-30. Every Original the player hadn't played gets 7 free messages. Originals released during the event get 7 more, and users who join mid-event get them too. OOC also gives 500 credits on sign-up and another 500 through referral codes. Episode's timers push players to start a second story while they wait for passes.
tactics.evidence: OOC's own copy frames it as a nudge toward Originals 'you haven't gotten around to yet', and it repeated the event right after Halloween. Of the OOC tactics on this list, this is the cheapest to copy. No outcome numbers are published.
tactics.effort: Low. A per-user, per-story allowance of free turns, plus a 'Free to try' badge on the shelf.
tactics.impact: Medium to High for D1 to D7. With 15-20 stories, the risk is that a user bounces off one story and never finds the one that hooks them. Pairing a free sample with each weekly release (tactic 3) also gives a reason to return.

tactics.tactic: 6. A replay and collection layer: visible stats, rarity-ranked endings, 'endings found x/y', and replaying from a branch
tactics.whatTheyDo: In OOC, each start setting can have up to 7 stats shown as live gauges and up to 10 endings rated N, R, SR or SSR, triggered by turn counts or stat thresholds. Opening an ending costs credits, and Session Branching lets players restart from any message. Character.AI Stories are built to be replayed for different endings. Linky bonding levels unlock custom greetings at level 2 and voice calls at level 4, and collectible cards come with the relationship. Talkie sells gacha pulls for character cards with gems.
tactics.evidence: OOC shipped Endings & Stats as one of its few named releases (v0.1.4, 2026-05-28) and Session Branching in September. Crack also supports branching from any point. Linky details come from a third-party review. None of these apps publish a retention lift for this.
tactics.effort: Low. Plotbreak already has rarity-ranked endings in the creator flow and the 'Ending Found' and 'Ending Hunter' badges. The work is surfacing them: an 'endings found 1/6' count and hints on story cards and the end screen, plus 'replay from this choice'.
tactics.impact: Medium to High. It multiplies hours per authored story, the key constraint with a 15-20 story catalog, and gives completers a reason to stay.

tactics.tactic: 7. Make the home feed re-slice the catalog many ways and change every day
tactics.whatTheyDo:
OOC's home (observed 2026-11-21) has:
- an event bar and a 6-slide rotating hero
- 16 genre and ranking tabs
- Top Ranked #1-20 with play counts and creator names
- Popular Originals, New Originals, and Trending Now #1-10
- Trending New Creators, tag chips, and New from certified creators
- a 'Today' tab of today's most-played titles
- seasonal rows such as 'Trick or Chat'
Talkie's main tabs are Chat, Creation Center and Trending. Webtoon groups titles by update weekday, sorted by views.
tactics.evidence: OOC's feed sits on 52,630 stories, but its structure is time windows (today, new, trending), ranks, counters and tags. Those work at 15-20 titles too. Its Today tab ranks titles with as few as 5 plays, which shows how much 'liveliness' comes from time-windowed ranking rather than volume.
tactics.effort: Low (UI plus queries). Today you have Top Ranked by likes, with seeded likes in production. Add 'Hot today' and 'This week' ranks by plays, New and UP badges, a rotating hero, 'Continue' and 'Because you played X' rows, tag shelves, live counters (plays, endings found) and a seasonal row.
tactics.impact: Medium. It improves first impressions and browse-to-play conversion, and it answers 'looks dead'. It cannot replace new content (tactic 3); without new titles the rows reshuffle the same 15-20 stories.

tactics.tactic: 8. A live-ops event every 1-2 weeks: seasonal skins, double rewards, limited-time content
tactics.whatTheyDo:
OOC's announcement cadence:
- Sale Week (Sep 1)
- A creator call for Halloween titles (Oct 19)
- A Halloween look, app icon and double check-in (Oct 25)
- Candy Packs and free messages (Oct 28)
- Daily Candy Pack sales (Oct 30)
- Free Messages (Nov 10-30)
Chapters ran an 8th-anniversary leaderboard challenge, outfit raffle and sale. Episode runs book clubs with reading challenges that pay rewards.
tactics.evidence: OOC's v0.1.27 release (Oct 27) is 'Halloween-exclusive content and a limited-time Halloween app theme'. OOC also sold a $111.99 Halloween Candy Pack in-app purchase and posts 2-3 announcements a week. No outcome numbers are published.
tactics.effort: Low per event once there is a template: a theme, a 2x reward, one limited story, a push, and a feed row. Plotbreak's Tower weekly free climb and streak bonus are already this kind of loop.
tactics.impact: Medium. Mostly reactivation of the installed base, plus fresh push copy. Smaller effect on new-user D1.

tactics.tactic: 9. Scale content supply: creator incentives plus an internal AI drafting pipeline (pay per picked story)
tactics.whatTheyDo: OOC's catalog is 52,630 stories versus 409 Originals, and community titles sit in its Top Ranked. Certified Creators get 2% of credits spent on their titles. The Originals program buys picked stories for $500 each plus a share, and now buys sequels too. Crack lets users build a world in about 5 minutes and pays KRW 300,000 plus a share for Crack Originals. Talkie's character remixing yielded tens of millions of user characters. Chai has 25M+ user-built AIs.
tactics.evidence: Chai: AI-assisted creation gave 56% higher-quality prompts and 33% more AIs created. Power users who train their own AIs get almost 2x the engagement of in-house ones. Episode: 150,000+ stories, mostly community-written. Janitor: 1.7M characters behind 2.5M daily users.
tactics.effort: High: moderation, tooling and payouts. Plotbreak already has a Create flow. At 30 installs/day there will be few creators, so near term this is the internal trend bot drafting stories for a human to polish. OOC's $200-500 per picked story is a reference price for buying outside stories.
tactics.impact: High long-term (catalog depth is what makes OOC feel alive) but Low to Medium in the next 1-2 months at current traffic.

tactics.tactic: 10. Social proof and referral loops: play counts on cards, follow creators, a shareable feed, two-sided referral credits
tactics.whatTheyDo: OOC shows plays and creator names on every card, has creator follows, launched a Profile Feed (2026-09-21) and added referral codes (2026-10-14): 500 credits for the new user, and 5% of their first-30-day purchases for the referrer. Character.AI launched a Feed on 2025-08-04 where users post chat snippets, scenes and videos that others can remix and continue. Linky has a 'Buzz' feed. Webtoon puts comments under every episode and asks readers to follow the creator after they subscribe. Episode has book clubs.
tactics.evidence: Character.AI's CEO pitched the Feed as a 'lean-back experience'. Users there average about 80 min/day (CEO, Aug 2025). OOC's referral reward is paid only on purchased credits and is capped at 100K credits a month. No retention lift is published for any of these.
tactics.effort: Low for referral credits and counters, Medium to High for a feed.
tactics.impact: Low to Medium at about 30 installs/day, because network effects need density. Referral credits and visible play counts are cheap and worth doing now; a social feed can wait.

benchmarks: Planning note (own calculation): with about 30 installs a day, an A/B test needs about 700 users per arm to see D7 move from 10% to 15% (80% power, alpha 0.05), which is 6-7 weeks of installs. Roll changes out one at a time and compare weekly cohorts rather than waiting on split tests.
